Policies in IAM A policy in IAM is a formal statement that defines what should happen regarding identities, access, or security. It's a governance directive , not just a technical rule. Policy Type Example Enforced via Access Policy "Only HR staff can access payroll data" Role mappings, ABAC SoD Policy "No user can both approve and request expenses" SoD matrix Authentication Policy "MFA required for admins" IAM config (e.g., Keycloak) Account Policy "Inactive users are disabled after 90 days" Lifecycle workflows Logging & Audit Policy "All access must be logged and retained" SIEM*, IAM audit logs Approval Policy "High-risk roles need 2-level approval" IGA workflow engine *SIEM: Security Information and Event Management

Role Lifecycle Management 1. Role Mining ( Discovery ) Focus: Analyze existing access patterns Outcome: Identify logical groupings of permissions and candidate roles 2. Role Definition ( Design ) Focus: Define business-friendly role names and descriptions Outcome: Create structured RBAC models, assign appropriate permissions to each role 3. Role Assignment ( Deployment ) Focus: Map users or groups to roles Outcome: Operationalize access control 4. Role Review ( Governance ) Focus: Periodically evaluate roles: · Are they still needed? · Are permissions still appropriate? Outcome: Ensure roles stay valid & minimal

Role Mining A network diagram with nodes and connections, overlaid on a background of concentric circles. Definition The process of discovering and designing roles based on existing user access patterns. Focus • Analyzing historical access data • Identifying common access combinations • Proposing logical roles to simplify and standardize permissions Purpose Create business-aligned roles from messy, individual entitlements Transition from ad hoc permissions to Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Role Definition: Designing Effective Access Roles Goal: Create clear, manageable roles that align with business functions. What to Define: • Role Name: Clear and business-readable (e.g., HR_Manager, Finance_Analyst) • Description: What is the purpose of this role? • Permissions: What resources and actions are included? • Scope: Is it department-wide, app-specific, or global? Types of Roles: • Business Roles: Align with job functions (e.g., Sales_Associate) • Technical Roles: Map to system permissions (e.g., DB_ReadOnly) • Composite Roles: Combine multiple roles into one (Keycloak supports this) Best Practices: • Use least privilege principle: no more access than needed • Avoid 'role explosion' (too many overly specific roles) • Reuse roles across systems if possible • Document everything clearly (owners, change process) Governance Tip: Roles should be reviewed and updated periodically to remain relevant and secure. What is Access Certification? Definition: Access Certification is a formal, recurring process where designated reviewers (e.g., managers or system owners) validate that users' access rights are appropriate and justified. Objective: Ensure that only authorized users retain access to systems and data Detect and remove outdated, excessive, or unauthorized access Meet regulatory and audit requirements (e.g., SOX, GDPR) Key Components: Review scope (users, systems, entitlements) Reviewers (managers, app owners, data owners) Attestation options (Approve, Revoke, Delegate) Justifications and comments Deadlines and escalation workflows Outcome: User System Access Reviewer Decision Justification Timestamp Alice HR System HR_Admin Bob Revoke No longer in HR 2025-06-03 10:15 AM Bob Finance Tool Viewer Clara Approve Needed for reporting 2025-06-03 10:18 AM Illustration of a woman in a business suit sitting at a desk, holding a tablet displaying a bar chart. Audit = Governance Process Audit refers to the systematic evaluation of IAM activities, controls, and compliance. It uses various data sources to determine: • Are access controls effective? • Are policies enforced? • Are users only accessing what they should? Inputs to IAM Audits Include: • Access logs (login, privilege use) • Role and permission assignments • Access certification results • SoD violation reports • User lifecycle events (join, move, leave) • Approval and workflow histories Outcome: Findings, risk analysis, compliance reports, recommendations.

Debrief: Audit Log Review Challenge Types of Anomalies to Flag: • Privilege escalation (e.g., Alice → Finance_Admin) • Brute force login attempt (e.g., Bob → 5 failed logins) • Suspicious account manipulation (e.g., Clara deletes, recreates, reassigns roles quickly) How to Correlate Events: • Time correlation: Clara's events occur within minutes • User behavior correlation: Bob's failed logins may signal compromise • Role sensitivity: High-privilege roles need extra scrutiny Compliance Report Highlights: Flag suspicious actions by Clara as potential policy violation Report failed login trend for Bob for follow-up or monitoring Review whether Alice's role assignment had proper approval Recommend logging justifications and better access change audit trails An illustration of a white tablet with a black magnifying glass resting on it. Discussion: Log Retention Dilemma You are designing IAM audit logging policies for a European company operating in financial services. Challenge: GDPR & SOX 1 GDPR requires data minimization and purposeful retention SOX requires access logs to be retained for 7 years Reconciling Requirements 2 What log types would you retain longer? How would you justify the retention legally? Would you anonymize or pseudonymize certain fields?
